tools.title: 5 Gadgets I Like ❤️
tools.summary_raw: I’ve been waking up to a gentler alarm, saving lines from books without my phone, and checking my focus with headphones. 5 gadgets I use, including limitations.
tools.content_text: The gadgets I find most interesting these days aren’t phones, laptops, or watches. Many don’t even have a screen. They just improve an everyday object. Here are five I’m finding useful, from a digital highlighter and headphones that measure my focus to a quiet alarm clock and a smart ball. Subscribe now Share Mark II — A Handy Digital Highlighter The Mark II is a digital highlighter that lets me scan and save passages from anything I’m reading. I drag it over my favorite lines in a book or magazine. Those highlights are automatically tagged and searchable in the Mark app, which is free to use with the highlighter. I also sync what I save to Readwise , which I use for organizing my highlights, including my favorite Kindle book passages and what I’ve saved from podcasts with the Snipd app. It’s become my central hub for everything I’ve clipped. I can query it from my AI tools like Claude and ChatGPT. In the past, I used my phone to scan book passages with the Readwise app. That worked well but required me to interrupt my reading with a screen. I appreciate that the Mark II feels more like a traditional highlighter than a phone. It has a useful voice note option: I can press a button to record my thoughts about whatever I’m reading. And it comes with a slim magnet that keeps it in your book. It’s not perfect, even if Time listed it as one of the Best Inventions of 2026 . I’ve often had to fill in words the Mark II skipped over. The app doesn’t signal that it might have missed words, so I’ve had to check passages on my phone for accuracy. And it’s slow to run over one line at a time. For a long passage that runs across multiple pages, the Readwise app is faster. Still, I like the Mark II’s design and I’m continuing to use it as a screenless way to save great sentences. Price: $159 is what I paid. It’s now on sale for $149. Neurable One — Headphones That Sense When I’m Fading These headphones have built-in sensors that assess my level of concentration. Like an EEG machine, they pick up electrical signals from my brain. In my testing, the readings generally lined up with how alert or tired I felt. When I’m doing deep work and my attention drops, the headphones play a chime. It’s a useful nudge to take a break. The accompanying app features games for practicing sustained attention. You can also use it to run experiments to see which behaviors deepen your focus, like going for a brisk walk or writing down a list of tasks you’re holding in your head. The headphones are comfortable and sound good for listening to podcasts or music. They don’t match my Sony XM6 headphones for noise canceling or battery life. I like using this Neurable headset, though, to see how long I can stick to a task before my mind wanders. It’s helped me notice when I’m sharpest during the day. Price: $449 on sale at the moment. $499 normally. No subscription cost. […]

market.title: How The Observer rebuilt its digital business with seven people and an AI agent
market.summary_raw: The Observer launched digital subscriptions in November 2025 and passed 70,000 within a year. In Oslo, Jack Riley, its Chief Customer Officer, told WAN-IFRA’s Newsroom Summit what it took: seven hires, an AI agent built on Claude and a single data analyst.
market.content_text: By John Rahim Executives at established publishers like to ask what they would build if they were starting today. The Observer has spent a year finding out. The Sunday title dates from 1791. When Tortoise Media bought it from the Guardian’s owner in April last year, it had never had a website of its own. Tortoise itself is a start-up built on podcasts, events and newsletters. Jack Riley , its Chief Customer Officer , told WAN-IFRA’s Newsroom Summit , held at the Norwegian publisher VG in Oslo, that he had inherited a famous brand and, on the digital side, a blank canvas. Digital subscriptions, new apps and a redesign arrived together on 27 November 2025. Less than a year later, Riley reported more than 70,000 subscribers. Revenue from digital customers has grown by an average of 30% a month for 11 months and now matches revenue from print subscriptions. Print has gained as well: subscriptions made up 36% of print sales last year and about 45% now. Riley gave no figures in pounds, and the match with print is with subscription revenue alone; newsstand sales are not included. A prospectus from 1791 still sets the brief The strategy starts with the first edition, which promised a paper free of prejudice and party, devoted to truth and to “every species of knowledge that may conduce to the happiness of society.” Riley reads that as a case for staying unbiased in a more polarised market, for breadth of coverage and for reporting that is constructive without pretending all is well. Against that brief he set three pressures, each with its own answer. The first is AI, which makes ordinary reporting easy to copy. The Observer’s answer is direct relationships with readers and original reporting that nobody else has. The second is a younger audience that would sooner watch or listen than read. The answer is Tortoise’s podcast business, now folded into the newsroom. The third is readers’ growing attachment to individual writers over the titles they write for. The answer is a newsroom reorganised around its best-known writers. The Observer’s hits under Tortoise include the investigation into The Salt Path , the bestselling memoir, and, in June, the scoop that Sir Keir Starmer was about to resign. The subscription must be worth more than the articles Every subscriber gets Culture Club , launched in the spring. It includes a weekly newsletter from Tim Adams, the Culture Editor; discounts negotiated with partners; events such as film screenings and Q&As with directors in the newsroom; and a book club that is also streamed online. Riley’s test is that a subscriber with a passing interest in culture who did nothing beyond taking up the offers would be “well served.” A subscription, he argued, is more likely to succeed when it offers much more than access to articles. Audio does similar work. […]

market.title: Draw the line at the story: Dietmar Schantin’s case for keeping narrative human
market.summary_raw: Let AI gather and sort the facts, the newsroom strategist told WAN-IFRA’s Newsroom Summit in Oslo, but keep the decision about what the story is with a named person. That accountability is what publishers still have to sell.
market.content_text: By John Rahim In the newsrooms Dietmar Schantin works with, one idea surfaces quickly once AI arrives: let the system write the first draft from the reporter’s notes and transcripts. He would rather it did not. Schantin, a strategist whose clients have included The Washington Post, The Wall Street Journal and The Telegraph, used his session at WAN-IFRA’s Newsroom Summit at VG in Oslo to argue that the decision turns on a commercial question: why do people come to a publisher, and why would they pay for what it does? His answer was to draw a line through the editorial process: AI can work on one side of it, and a named person is responsible for everything on the other. Publishers supply the answers and lose the reader The commercial problem shows up in the numbers. Gallup’s latest poll puts American trust in the mass media at 33%, up from the 28% cited in Schantin’s new book, The Architecture of Journalism in the Age of AI , though he noted that the rise came from Republicans. SparkToro’s analysis found that 68% of Google searches in America ended without a click in the first four months of this year. Chartbeat’s data show chatbots sending publishers less than 1% of their pageviews, so little of the traffic lost at the search page is coming back by another route. A reader who gets the answer from an assistant that draws on a publisher’s reporting never meets that publisher’s paywall. Drawing on slides from Greg Piechota, Schantin cited an estimate that publishers lose 10% of their potential subscription sign-ups this way and said he thought the true figure was higher. A court has begun asking who answers for a summary What is changing, in his reading, is that someone is being held to account for machine-written text. In May, the Munich regional court granted an injunction against Google after its AI Overviews tied two Munich publishers to scams that none of the linked sources mentioned; the court treated the summary as Google’s own statement. In January, the Guardian reported that overviews on liver blood tests gave normal ranges without the context a patient would need to interpret them. Google removed some of them, and Schantin said similar queries still return the same kind of summaries. Publishers ought to profit from being the source that is correct and answerable, and some are making that harder for themselves. In April, The New York Times published a remark attributed to Pierre Poilievre, Canada’s Conservative leader, that turned out to be an AI-generated summary rendered as a quotation. A reader caught it, Schantin observed, and the correction took more than two weeks. Press Gazette now keeps a running tracker of such cases. Generative models work on probability, he said, so the errors will never go away. Dietmar Schantin at Newsroom Summit in Oslo. Photo by Tom Atle Bordevik / Bordevik.no Where the line goes: a fifth layer called narrative If the errors will not go away, the question becomes where AI should stop. […]

market.title: Newsletters, obits, and the world’s longest yard sale: How some local news sites saw their traffic spike
market.summary_raw: It’s time for our latest look at which newsrooms are having success increasing their web traffic. We bring you four of these each quarter, looking at four different market segments: local newspapers, nonprofit news outlets, public media stations, and for-profit local news sites. Rankings are based on estimates from Similarweb. Today’s edition looks at local...
market.content_text: It’s time for our latest look at which newsrooms are having success increasing their web traffic . We bring you four of these each quarter, looking at four different market segments: local newspapers, nonprofit news outlets, public media stations, and for-profit local news sites. Rankings are based on estimates from Similarweb . Today’s edition looks at local for-profit news sites . (Eligible sites for this ranking are for-profit members of the trade group LION Publishers — LION standing for Local, Independent, Online News — so these are mostly digital-born newsrooms, not newspapers or TV stations.) The rankings for Q3 feature many of the same sites that performed well in our last edition . This time around, we’ve got details from local news sites in New York, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Nevada, Georgia, and Oregon. Below that are the Top 25 rankings for July, August, and September. W42ST In New York’s Hell’s Kitchen, W42ST has been covering neighborhood news since 2014. Its traffic jumped 84% from June to July. Publisher Phil O’Brien said that boost is attributable to one day’s traffic to a single story: this story on the deaths, four days apart, of Jeffrey Newman and Jayson Conner , a couple who ran Backpacks for the Street, a charity that offered supplies to those living on the city’s streets. W42ST published its story on July 11; a few hours later, The New York Times ran its own obituary , and thousands of people who read that piece went to Google to find out more. Visits on July 12 were roughly 10 times a normal Sunday on W42ST. “A spike like this is lovely, but it doesn’t pay the bills,” O’Brien told me over email. He noted that the average reader of that story who came from search was engaged for 26 seconds; readers who came to it from W42ST’s own newsletter averaged more than three and a half minutes. “A reader from across the country who spends 26 seconds on an obituary is welcome, but they’re not who we’re building for.” O’Brien was writing to me from England, where he’s currently trying to bring W42ST’s hyperlocal model to the town of Southport (O’Brien was born in Liverpool). Stand Up For Southport is a six-year-old site that received a government Local News Fund grant to expand operations, and O’Brien is spending a few months there to offer his W42ST-bred expertise. The new daily newsletter they’ve launched earned more than 1,000 subs in the first week. It’s a nice reversal from just four years ago, when O’Brien had his American visa renewal application rejected because immigration officials declared W42ST was a “marginal” business. He spent the next five months running the site from London. “The idea is a hyperlocal model that can travel,” he said. Point/Plover Metro Wire Wisconsin’s Point/Plover Metro Wire describes itself as the only locally owned and operated daily news source in Portage County, and the county is the only place it covers. market.title: An open laptop, a crowded Orange Line train, and a tipster
market.summary_raw: Is “seen on the Orange Line” the new “overheard on the Acela”? ProPublica reported on potential plans to overhaul the Smithsonian on Monday. Alec MacGillis and Andy Kroll wrote that the plans, if enacted, “would represent an unprecedented assertion of White House control over the Smithsonian, which is structured to be independent.” But how did...
market.content_text: Is “seen on the Orange Line” the new “overheard on the Acela”? ProPublica reported on potential plans to overhaul the Smithsonian on Monday. Alec MacGillis and Andy Kroll wrote that the plans, if enacted, “would represent an unprecedented assertion of White House control over the Smithsonian, which is structured to be independent.” But how did MacGillis and Kroll get their hands on the explosive 25-item list? An open laptop, a crowded D.C. Metro train, and a quick-thinking tipster. From the ProPublica piece: In the last week of October, as political Washington was focused on the coming midterm elections, a commuter on the Orange Line from the Northern Virginia suburbs was startled to see displayed, on the laptop of a man seated adjacent in a gray tartan suit, a document titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan.” The commuter snapped a few phone photos over the man’s shoulder and dispatched them to ProPublica. The ProPublica reporters, going off initials seen on the laptop, searched White House staffing records and “took to the Orange Line,” hoping it was a regular route for the staffer. Sure enough, there we saw the likeliest candidate, carrying the same style of brown leather satchel and same type of phone. He disembarked in Washington for the short walk to a White House employee checkpoint. Kroll told me that he and MacGillis made three trips to different parts of the Orange Line to report out the tip. “That included me standing outside for a few hours in a Metro station on an especially cold morning with a woefully insufficient coat on,” Kroll added. “Not the most glamorous reporting assignment, but important to getting the story.” We’ve covered ProPublica’s creative attempts to reach prospective tipsters — which include an LED billboard truck and public transit ads in the Washington, D.C. area — in the past. The nonprofit investigative outlet has been a news industry leader in crowdsourcing and engagement reporting. ProPublica engagement and tips coordinator Adriana Pera told me that the tips line has been “very, very busy.” In November, ProPublica received its “highest number of tips to date,” Pera said. At least 20 ProPublica investigations in the last year started with sensitive information delivered through the tips line. “We have to attribute some of this surge to our efforts to get out into the world and show people that we’re listening and that they can trust us with their knowledge — from working with ad companies in Washington, D.C., to get our tips line on bus shelters, to flyering outside of conferences, and events with sources that could help our reporting needs,” she said. During a recent conference for the Association of the United States Army (AUSA), the largest annual gathering of Army contractors, Pera and others handed out flyers. ProPublica also purchased ads on bus shelters they thought attendees were likely to walk by. […]
